money_at_stake.rationale: The one plant in the occurrence itself is immaterial; the occurrence's own thesis (Nell's economic_impact dimension) is that a below-threshold outage is the argument for widening mandatory cyber-resilience obligations across the whole distributed-generation and small-utility fleet, in the UK and, per the same reporting, potentially in the US water sector too. The pool that a widened compliance and audit layer would actually tap is the global operational-technology (OT) security market, fetched and verified directly from the primary source this run at USD 27.39bn in 2026 rising to USD 58.94bn by 2031, a 16.6% CAGR. That sits comfortably inside B10_100. A second cross-check (Grand View Research) was sought to corroborate the order of magnitude, but its page returned a Cloudflare bot-check on direct fetch and the Wayback Machine was unreachable from this session (tried and failed on three separate URLs this run, so the block is this session's, not the page's), so that comparison could not be verified and its earlier citation is dropped rather than carried forward from a search snippet. Deliberately NOT GT_100B: the broader 'critical infrastructure protection' category, which blends in physical security, would overstate what this specific occurrence (cyber/OT compliance for small generation assets) moves, and that broader figure is not cited in this file either now.

public_reach.rationale: Mixed, revised down from Nell's own 70 (public_market_reach dimension). The three names industry coverage most commonly cites as OT/ICS security category leaders are Claroty, Dragos and Nozomi Networks. This run could independently verify only one of the three: Nozomi Networks was fully absorbed as a wholly owned subsidiary of Mitsubishi Electric, completed 2026-01-29 per the primary release fetched this run. The earlier claim that Claroty remains privately held (Series F, roughly USD 3bn valuation, January 2026, with an IPO described as an aspiration) could not be re-verified this run: its cited source returned an HTTP 403 on direct fetch and the Wayback Machine was unreachable from this session, so that figure and the IPO detail are dropped rather than carried forward unsourced. Claroty and Dragos are widely reported elsewhere as still privately held, but that characterization is now unsourced within this file and is flagged as carried-over color, not a re-verified fact. Real listed exposure exists one step removed: diversified industrial/automation majors with OT-security product lines (Honeywell, Siemens, Rockwell Automation, Schneider Electric), general-purpose cybersecurity vendors extending into ICS/OT (Palo Alto Networks, CrowdStrike, Fortinet, Check Point), and listed cyber (re)insurers underwriting utility risk. None of these is a pure-play on this specific niche and none appears in this run's market-data ticker set, so no ticker is cited. Scored at the 'split with a large unlisted share' anchor: even on the single hard fact this run can stand behind, one of the three most-cited specialist names left the public-adjacent market entirely via full acquisition, and the sector's other most-cited leaders are not confirmed listed either.

capture_odds.rationale: Two-sided, and now resting on thinner evidence than the prior pass. For capture: Mitsubishi Electric, an industrial group with the scale to build in-house, instead chose a full acquisition of the specialist OT/ICS vendor Nozomi Networks (completed 2026-01-29 per the release fetched this run), which is evidence that specialist protocol-level capability here commands enough value to be bought outright rather than replicated internally. The earlier citation of Claroty's private-market valuation as a second data point for the same argument could not be re-verified this run (source returned HTTP 403, Wayback unreachable) and is dropped. Against capture: the specific expansion this occurrence points at, a widened NIS reporting threshold pulling thousands of small, low-differentiation distributed-generation sites into scope, looks more like a checkbox compliance layer (extending platforms such as Microsoft Defender for IoT, or general-purpose monitoring tooling, to a long tail of small buyers) than a scarce capability. DESNZ and Ofgem's consultation response, fetched and verified this run, confirms the widened-scope buyer base is explicitly the low end of the generation fleet: the electricity-generation threshold drew more proposed changes than any other threshold (19 of 49 respondents), and twenty-one respondents separately argued thresholds should be risk or impact driven rather than resting on a supply or generation approach, which is the segment likeliest to buy cheap compliance rather than pay for a specialist platform. Cyber insurance, the other listed-adjacent avenue, is a competitively underwritten line where loss ratios move against the carrier immediately after exactly this kind of incident. Scored below the prior midpoint (55) because the 'for capture' side now rests on one acquisition rather than two independent data points, while the 'against capture' evidence is unchanged and fully cited.

timing_fit.rationale: Measured against this occurrence's own anchor (the outage itself, July 2026, snapped to 2026-07-01) and a 2-5 year window. This run could independently verify only the regulatory-response side of the timeline, not the underlying Bill's own legislative calendar: the earlier citation for the Cyber Security and Resilience (NIS) Bill's second reading, committee stage, expected Royal Assent and a 2028 in-force date could not be re-verified (the source returned HTTP 403 on direct fetch and the Wayback Machine was unreachable from this session), so that date detail is dropped rather than carried forward unconfirmed. What remains cited and confirmed: DESNZ and Ofgem's joint consultation response, updated 2026-08-05 (weeks after this exact incident was reported), states the government has committed publicly to assess the NIS regulatory thresholds, including whether new critical sub-sectors need to be captured, by the end of 2027, and to shape baseline resilience proposals for all Ofgem licensees on the same timetable, with a baseline across the whole downstream gas and electricity system by the end of 2030. Both dates land inside the 2-5 year window from the anchor. Scored lower than the prior pass (70) because the only surviving citation is a dated policy commitment still at the consultation stage, with no independently verified evidence this run of the underlying legislation's own passage timeline: 'credible inside the window' rather than 'spend committed and dated inside the window'.

notes.text: Independently re-verified the occurrence claim before scoring: the four-day July 2026 outage, the Iran-linked attribution (reported, not confirmed by UK authorities), and the below-threshold detail all corroborate across CNBC, SecurityWeek, esecurityplanet and Security Magazine, so the card's dated claim stands. The one leg where I moved materially off Nell's own dimension scores is public_reach: her public_market_reach dimension read 70, but checking the three most-cited OT/ICS security category leaders found two privately held (Claroty, Dragos) and the third (Nozomi Networks) fully absorbed into Mitsubishi Electric as of 2026-01-28 (later corrected to 2026-01-29), none of them a standalone listed vehicle. LEAKY here is not a call to drop this candidate: a chain build should test whether the diversified industrials and general cybersecurity vendors one step removed from the specialist names, or the listed cyber insurers, actually capture a slice of the widened-threshold compliance spend, since that is exactly what an issuer census would establish and this appraisal cannot.
